title: Too Small to See, Still Alive

scenes.visual: Clear pond water drop with a question mark; a microscope view of it shows tiny outlined living things drifting; the question appears.
scenes.tts: A drop of pond water can look completely clear. Put it under a microscope, and you may see tiny living things swimming and turning. How can we know something is alive if it is too small to see?
scenes.narration: A drop of pond water can look completely clear. Put it under a microscope, and you may see tiny living things swimming and turning. How can we know something is alive if it is too small to see?

scenes.visual: A one millimetre bar; its first tenth lights up, then is enlarged to show tiny cells inside, not to scale.
scenes.tts: Your eyes have a limit. Most people cannot see an object smaller than about one tenth of a millimetre. A micrometre is one thousandth of a millimetre. So the limit is about one hundred micrometres. Most cells are smaller than that.
scenes.narration: Your eyes have a limit. Most people cannot see an object smaller than about 0.1 mm. A micrometre (µm) is one thousandth of a millimetre. So the limit is about 100 µm. Most cells are smaller than that.
scenes.caption: Your eyes have a limit. Most people cannot see an object smaller than about 0.1 mm. A micrometre (µm) is one thousandth of a millimetre. So the limit is about 100 µm. Most cells are smaller than that.

scenes.visual: A small sample passes a lens and appears larger; then the eyepiece and three objective chips multiply into three totals.
scenes.tts: A microscope is a tool with lenses. It makes small things look larger. Magnification is how many times larger the image looks than the real thing. A school microscope has an eyepiece that magnifies ten times. Its objective lenses are often four, ten, and forty times. Multiply them. That gives forty, one hundred, or four hundred times in all.
scenes.narration: A microscope is a tool with lenses. It makes small things look larger. Magnification is how many times larger the image looks than the real thing. A school microscope has an eyepiece that magnifies 10 times (10x). Its objective lenses are often 4x, 10x, and 40x. Multiply them. That gives 40x, 100x, or 400x in all.

scenes.visual: A log size axis in micrometres: the eye's limit, the light microscope's limit, and an arrow toward smaller sizes for the electron microscope.
scenes.tts: A light microscope can show details down to about zero point two micrometres. That is enough to see most whole cells. Later, scientists built the electron microscope. It uses a beam of electrons, not light. It showed cell parts far too small for any light microscope.
scenes.narration: A light microscope can show details down to about 0.2 µm. That is enough to see most whole cells. Later, scientists built the electron microscope. It uses a beam of electrons, not light. It showed cell parts far too small for any light microscope.

scenes.visual: One outlined cell; the three parts appear as numbered cards, each with its own picture: one cell and many cells, the basic unit, a cell coming from a cell.
scenes.tts: A cell is the smallest unit that can carry out the processes of life. The cell theory sums up what scientists have learned about cells. It has three parts. First, all living things are made of one or more cells. Second, the cell is the basic unit of life. Third, all cells come from cells that already exist.

scenes.visual: Theory defined, guess crossed out; tools feed evidence into the cell theory; then the clear drop, the microscope and the cells it shows.
scenes.tts: In science, a theory is a well-tested explanation backed by a great deal of evidence. It is not a guess. The cell theory grew as better microscopes gave new evidence. So how do we know something is alive when it is too small to see? A microscope makes it look large enough to see. It shows that each one is made of one or more cells.
